title: Lehna becomes Angad
hook: Nanak names Lehna his successor and calls him Angad, part of my own body

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sheet of flowers, and the Guru who belonged to no one side. Your line was flowers for everyone. Where did you find an answer that gave something to both? Day forty-four.

When a founder steps down, the next in line can seem obvious. The eldest son takes over the family shop. The deputy gets the corner office. Guru Nanak had two grown sons. The elder, Sri Chand, was a deeply devout man, an ascetic who had renounced ordinary life. The younger, Lakhmi Das, was a householder with a family. Either would have been the obvious choice. But for years Nanak had been watching someone else: the trader who'd carried the wet grass, cleared the ditch and fished the bowl out of dirty water. Today we step back a little in time, to a few months before the flowers, and the day Nanak made his choice.
screen: `EVERYONE ASSUMES THE SON.` → `TWO SONS, BOTH DEVOUT.` → `THE GURU WAS WATCHING SOMEONE ELSE.`

segments.voice: Tradition says Nanak placed a coconut and five copper coins before Lehna and bowed to him. The teacher bowed to the student. Then he gave him a new name: Angad. And that name is today's word, inside it. Ang means a limb, a part of the body. So Angad is often explained as part of my own body. The Guru was saying: this man isn't my replacement, he's me, continued. There's a line in the scripture, in a ballad sung by two of the Gurus' musicians, Satta and Balvand, that says it plainly. The light was the same, the way was the same; the king had only changed his body. That's the Sikh understanding of the ten Gurus. Not ten different teachers with ten different messages, but one light, passed from one body to the next, like a flame lit from a flame. Which is why the Gurus whose hymns are in the scripture signed them not with their own names but with Nanak's. And one more turn of the word. Ang also names the pages of the Sikh scripture. You don't say page 360 of the Guru Granth Sahib; you say Ang 360. Each page is a limb of the Guru. So the word that named the second Guru now names every page of the book the Sikhs call their Guru today. One more thing to notice: Nanak didn't choose by blood. He chose the one who had become a servant. The light went to the one who could carry it, and it's still traveling.
screen: `THE TEACHER BOWED TO THE STUDENT.` · `ANG — A LIMB, PART OF THE BODY.` · `ONE LIGHT, A NEW BODY.` · `ANG — EVERY PAGE OF THE SCRIPTURE.` · then, large: `PASSING THE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think who carries your work on. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you care about: a skill, a family recipe, a way of doing your job, a value your parents gave you. Who is going to carry it after you? A child, a colleague, a friend, a student. See their face. If nobody comes to mind, notice that too, and wonder who it might be. The bell holds the time.
Ang. A limb, a part of the body; inside the name Angad, and the word Sikhs use for every page of their scripture. Today's word.
Your line: passing the light. Today, teach one thing you know to someone who could carry it on. Day forty-four.

howItsDone: Sikhs understand the ten Gurus as one light passing through ten bodies, and they refer to the pages of the Guru Granth Sahib as angs, limbs of the Guru; Guru Angad's accession is remembered each year.

original.note: Gurmukhi: ang, a limb or part of the body; Angad, part of me; and each page of the Guru Granth Sahib.

trapdoor: what you thought: a man got a new name.
what it means: one light passed to a new body; the second Guru is Nanak continued.
what a scholar hears: Satta and Balvand's ballad, around Ang 966, says the light and the way were the same, only the body changed; and ang still names each page.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ramkali ki Var of Satta and Balvand, Ang 966 (the same light, the body changed)

notes: Coconut and five copper coins (paise) placed before Lehna: common tradition; Bhai Buddha applying the tilak is omitted. Confirm.
Satta and Balvand's var line 'joti oha jugati saai sahi kaaiaa pheri paltteeai' at Ang 966; paraphrased. Confirm Ang.
Etymology: Angad commonly explained as 'part of my own body' (ang + ad/apna); confirm the explanation.
Date of succession (1539, shortly before Nanak's death) left unstated; 'a few months before the flowers' is approximate. Confirm.
Sri Chand described as ascetic (founder of the Udasi order, not named here); Lakhmi Das as householder. Confirm.
